corrected_claim: McPherson farm, 1 Jul: a garden with a picket fence stood at the house yard when the 147th NY halted there (no hour given); Col. Stone, wounded while his brigade held the ridge (about 11:00 to about 15:30), was carried into the stone basement barn on the south side of the pike, and the NPS records that the 1st Corps sheltered its wounded in the farm buildings on 1 Jul and that they stayed full of Union wounded under Confederate control; the barn survived the battle. Most pike fences were destroyed (6,844 rails claimed) and rail piles were built on the afternoon of 1 Jul from field and pike fences.

subclaims.claim: A garden with a picket fence stood at the McPherson House yard on 1 Jul: the 147th NY (Lt. Col. Miller) halted near it, a few rods east of the stone basement barn on the south side of the pike, before the regiment was sent to the railroad cut; the source gives no clock hour.
subclaims.why: Regimental history of the 147th NY (1902, retrospective): unit, place, object and day are in the quote and its section; the hour of the halt is not stated, so the "forenoon" of the first close-out is withdrawn.

subclaims.claim: The McPherson barn was a stone basement barn on the south side of the Chambersburg pike on 1 Jul; the OR calls it "McPherson's barn" (Dwight) and "a house and barn on the Chambersburg pike" (Wister).

Col. Roy Stone was wounded in the engagements of 1 Jul, while his brigade held the McPherson Ridge line from about 11:00 until it was ordered to retire at about 15:30, and was carried into the barn "before spoken of" (the house and barn on the Chambersburg pike); the NPS records that the farm buildings "were used by the 1st Corps to shelter the wounded on July 1".
subclaims.why: Wister (OR) names the barn and the wounding; the 149th PA narrative gives the brigade's hours on the field (about 11:00 to about 15:30), which bound the first use of the barn to the daytime of 1 Jul, earlier than the printed "evening". The OR does not call it a hospital.

subclaims.claim: The McPherson farm buildings were not burned or lost in the battle: "the farmhouse, bank barn, stables, and wagon shed withstood the fighting" (NPS CLR); the loss of the farmhouse (1896), wagon shed, orchard and barnyard (to about 1904) came afterwards (NPS CLI).
subclaims.why: Institutional secondary statements (NPS CLR, NPS CLI, NPS Historical Statement); no primary text states an absence of loss, none exists to quote.

subclaims.claim: The printed "Evening Jul 1" is not the opening of the aid-station use: Stone was carried into the barn while the brigade was on the field (about 11:00 to about 15:30), and the buildings "remained filled with Union wounded while the area was under Confederate control" (so they were an aid station through the evening and after).
subclaims.why: Hours from the 149th PA narrative (brigade on the field) and Wister (Stone carried into the barn); the evening state from the NPS CLR. No source fixes an hour for a "formal" aid station.

subclaims.claim: Most of the fences along the Chambersburg Pike at the McPherson farm had been destroyed by the end of the battle; Edward McPherson claimed the loss of 6,844 rails, 20 feet of boards and 138 posts over the whole farm.
subclaims.why: NPS summary of the claim file; no date or hour within the three days and no fence-by-fence extent (the claim covers the whole farm).

subclaims.claim: On the afternoon of 1 Jul Col. Roy Stone's color guard sheltered behind two rail piles forming a right angle; the rails had been carried together from a fence on the eastern boundary of a wheat field (McPherson Field 7) and from the pike to an old railroad cut north of it.
subclaims.why: NPS report quoting a battle account; the identity of the account is in the report's footnote 39 (not read here). It documents rails taken from the pike fences and a field boundary fence of the McPherson farm on the afternoon of 1 Jul.

corrected_claim: Town buildings passed to Confederate control on the evening of 1 Jul (Early p.469; Schurz p.730); Pennsylvania Hall carried a Union signal officer at 08:30 (Jacobs) and served Lee as an observation post on 3 Jul while a hospital (Jacobs); its own change of control on 1 Jul evening is not documented.

subclaims.claim: The town was entered by the enemy as the Union troops fell back through it after 5 p.m. on 1 Jul (Schurz) and Early's division (Hays' brigade) fought its way in and formed in the main street (Early); the clock hour of Early's entry is not stated.
subclaims.why: Early (OR27-2 p.469) gives no hour; Schurz (OR27-1 p.730) dates the withdrawal to Cemetery Hill after 5 o'clock and says the enemy entered the town immediately after the Union troops.

subclaims.claim: Early on 1 Jul the hills round Gettysburg had been examined by "the General" (Howard, named two sentences earlier) and his signal officers; at 08:30 one of them was on the College cupola making observations.
subclaims.why: Prof. Jacobs, eyewitness; names the College cupola, not the building name "Pennsylvania Hall" (see S-018.4).

subclaims.claim: On 3 Jul (Jacobs's heading "Friday, July 3") General Lee reconnoitred the Union position from the College cupola although, as Jacobs notes, the building was a hospital.
subclaims.why: Jacobs places it on 3 Jul. This does not date the loss of Union control (the printed "evening 1 Jul") of the building itself.

subclaims.claim: The "College cupola" of Jacobs is the cupola of Pennsylvania Hall, "the College Edifice" of Gettysburg College, which the NPS says served in the battle as an observation post, signal station and hospital; Bachelder (1873) says the College building was a Confederate hospital "during, and for some time after the battle".
subclaims.why: The NPS and Bachelder name the college building and its battle uses; the link between the words "College cupola" and Pennsylvania Hall is the shared name "the College", not a text that says "Pennsylvania Hall".

sub_requirement_text: State-schedule entry S-020 changes state at its documented window.
corrected_claim: Cemetery Hill: stone walls and fences enclosed the cemetery and hill when XI Corps took position after 5 p.m. on 1 Jul (Schurz, Einsiedel, Dobke, Steinwehr); batteries threw up light earthworks in front of each gun at dusk on 1 Jul (Wainwright, Hunt); the 88th PA built a rail-and-earth breastwork on the left of the hill that evening (Patterson). Wall layout stays open (fence-2-EG-07).

subclaims.claim: The XI Corps took position on Cemetery Hill after 5 o'clock on 1 Jul, its Second Division (Steinwehr) "behind the stone walls inclosing the cemetery on the west side".

A "square" stone fence stood at the cemetery about 1 mile from Gettysburg, to the right of the road from Baltimore to Gettysburg; the 41st NY bivouacked behind it at about 22:00 on 1 Jul and six companies took position on it at 04:00 on 2 Jul; the 45th NY rallied "behind the stone fence" at the cemetery on the evening of 1 Jul (no hostile demonstration that night).
Stone fences surrounded the hill and sheltered the infantry (Steinwehr's division) during the heavy bombardment that began about 16:00 on 2 Jul and lasted two hours.

At dusk on 1 Jul (Wainwright) the batteries on the hill outside the cemetery gate were posted with light earthworks thrown up in front of each gun to protect the men from the sharpshooters; Hunt describes the same posting after the retreat through the town ("Each of the guns in these batteries had a small earthwork thrown up in its front") without an hour.
subclaims.why: Wainwright (Artillery Brigade, First Corps) gives the hour ("At dusk"); Hunt (Chief of Artillery) gives the same fact in the sequence of the retreat of 1 Jul. Builders are not named (the batteries' own men are implied by "to protect the men").

subclaims.claim: After falling back through the town on 1 Jul the 88th PA took a position "on the left of the hill, which was afterward the center of the line of battle", and "threw up breastworks made of rails and earth" (the diary entry that follows is dated 3 Jul); the source of the rails is not stated.
subclaims.why: Capt. Patterson commanded the 88th PA (R054); the date follows from the sequence of his report (retreat through the town, then the position); the unit is not on Cemetery Hill proper.

subclaims.claim: In July 1863 Evergreen Cemetery had "60 family plots enclosed by ornamental iron fences", about 500 marble and granite monuments and headstones, a pumphouse gazebo and "the prominent brick gatehouse along Baltimore Pike"; "Much of the landscape had been damaged in the fighting".
subclaims.why: Institutional secondary (NPS Cultural Landscape Report); the passage describes the July 1863 landscape.

subclaims.claim: Stone (and wood) fences bordered the four fields of the national cemetery site along Baltimore Pike, Steinwehr Avenue and Taneytown Road; troops used them as breastworks, extended the wall along the north side of the Menchy field out into Baltimore Pike (probably the 82nd Ohio) and may have added perpendicular extensions as traverses in the Pierce field (NPS): positions, lengths and heights of the segments are not given.
subclaims.why: NPS secondary statement with "probably" and "may have"; no segment survey.

subclaims.claim: Occupied and fortified across "Jul 1 afternoon-night" (printed).
subclaims.why: Occupation after 5 p.m. documented; works at dusk documented for the guns; no works documented for infantry other than the 88th PA rail breastwork.

corrected_claim: Confederate sharpshooters occupied houses and steeples of public buildings in the town during the night of 1-2 Jul and fired on Cemetery Hill on 2 and 3 Jul (Willis, Farnham, Harris, Smith); a church steeple is named by a battery history; Union troops answered from a stone church and houses (Steinwehr). subclaims.claim: Confederate sharpshooters held houses in the town and fired on the Union line on Cemetery Hill: posted in houses and steeples during the night of 1-2 Jul and firing on 2 Jul (Willis), from windows and houses about 21:00 on 2 Jul (Farnham), from buildings on the outskirts on 3 Jul (Harris); Smith places sharpshooters in the houses of the town in the period when the skirmishers were engaged "from the 1st to the night of July 3"; Steinwehr put regiments into a large stone church and houses to counter them.
subclaims.why: Five OR reports, each with its own place and hour; the dating of the posts to the night of 1-2 Jul is Willis alone.

subclaims.claim: The sharpshooters were already in their posts at the start of 2 Jul: Willis says they "during the night had couched themselves in houses and steeples of public buildings" and "harassed us constantly" the next day; the exact hour of dawn is not stated.
subclaims.why: Replaces the printed "from dawn 2 Jul"; the posts date from the night of 1-2 Jul.

subclaims.claim: Sharpshooters were posted in a steeple of the town (Wiedrich's battery: "the church steeple") and in "steeples of public buildings" (Willis); no source names the Sweney house or the word belfry.
subclaims.why: Two independent witnesses (an OR report and a battery history); the printed "church belfry" is supported as a steeple, the "Sweney House" is not.

subclaims.claim: Sniper post in the Sweney house.
subclaims.why: "Sweney" in OR27 is Maj. J. W. Sweeney of Jenkins' cavalry; in the NPS CLR the Sweney family are owners of the Harman farm on the Chambersburg Pike; no local text places a sniper post in a Sweney house in the town.

printed.time: About 06:00 to 09:00-10:00 (to about noon, flag) Jul 2

corrected_claim: Culp's Hill, 2 Jul: Geary's division was placed "At 5 a. m."; Greene's brigade was in line at about 06:00 (60th and 78th NY; the 149th NY marched at about 04:00) and began breastworks of logs, cord-wood, stones and earth at once by Greene's order. Finish: "By 12 o'clock" (Greene, read from the page image: the OCR prints 13), about noon (137th NY, Ireland) and about 09:00 (60th NY, Godard): two values, 09:00 and 12:00, carried as scenarios. A stone wall stood behind the First Division's line when it formed (30-75 yd behind its works, four witnesses) and Geary and Greene place a wall 200-300 yd behind Kane's works, held by the enemy on the night of 2 Jul; one wall or two is not stated. Line length: no source.

subclaims.claim: Greene's brigade took position on the crest of Culp's Hill on the morning of 2 Jul at about 06:00 ("we took position at about G a. m.", OCR digit read as 6; Col. Godard, 60th NY: "at or about 6 a. m."; Lieut. Col. von Hammerstein, 78th NY: "about 6 o'clock"), the 149th NY having marched at about 04:00 (Barnum); the division as a whole "At 5 a. m. on the 2d" was placed on the right of the centre of the line (Geary).
subclaims.why: Hour 05:00 (division, Geary) to 06:00 (brigade, three reports); the first digit in Greene's report is OCR-read, the other reports give 6 in clear text. Greene 1893: "At sunrise we marched to the extreme right".

subclaims.claim: Greene's brigade began to intrench "as soon as we were in position", by Greene's order ("by order of General Greene, in person commanding Third Brigade", Godard), and built breastworks "of the covering height, of logs, cord-wood, stones, and earth"; regiment accounts: "trees and dirt" (78th NY), "stones, logs, rails, and earth" (149th NY); Geary's whole line did the same "immediately".

Greene's report: "By 12 o'clock we had a good cover for the men" (the text file's OCR prints "13"; the printed page, read from the archive.org page image of printed p.856, says 12); Greene 1893: "in a few hours we had a good breast-work" and "completed early in the day, almost exclusively by the Third Brigade".
subclaims.why: The digit is read from the page image (see image_reading on the citation); the OCR quote is kept so that the offsets stay valid. It agrees with Ireland (137th NY, about noon) and differs from Godard (60th NY, about 09:00).

subclaims.claim: A stone wall stood behind the First Division's line when its brigades formed on 2 Jul and was repaired, not built, by them: "A thick stone fence parallel to the ridge, less than 50 yards behind it" (Williams); "about 75 yards" behind the First Brigade's breastworks (Ruger); the brigade formed "our rear line behind a stone wall, our front line parallel to the stone wall and about 40 paces in advance" and then "immediately built breastworks" (McDougall); "some 125 feet in rear of the first line", repaired by the 145th NY (Price): 30-75 yd for four witnesses (125 ft = 42 yd; 40 paces is about 30-33 yd by our conversion). Geary places a stone wall "about 200 yards in rear of" Ruger's and Kane's intrenchments and Greene "about 300 yards in its rear" of Kane's line, held by the enemy on the night of 2 Jul.
subclaims.why: Four First Division witnesses agree within 30-75 yd for the wall behind McDougall's brigade; two Second Division witnesses give 200-300 yd for a wall held by the enemy that night. Whether these are one wall or two is not stated by any source: the distances stay selectable scenarios (no default).

subclaims.claim: The 145th NY (Col. Price, First Brigade, second line) repaired the stone wall behind the line during 2 Jul until 18:30, while the regiments of the first line built breastworks.

The 3rd Wisconsin (Col. Hawley) took position on the east bank of Rock Creek on 2 Jul, threw up breastworks of earth and rails and threw down such stone walls and fences in its front as might give the enemy cover, and rested behind its works until 18:00; the Third Brigade's whole line had "breastworks of rails, timber, and stone" thrown up "speedily" (Col. Colgrove, commanding the brigade).

On the night of 2 Jul the enemy held the First Division's whole original intrenched line and the stone fence (Williams), and the stone wall about 200 yards behind Ruger's and Kane's intrenchments "as a protection against attack from the direction of the turnpike" (Geary); Greene, at the close of the night attack, found the enemy posted behind the stone wall about 300 yards behind Kane's line.
The line was about 300 yd long on the morning of 2 Jul.
subclaims.why: Only source GD-219 (a blog); no OR or regimental text gives a length.

subclaims.claim: The 137th NY (Col. Ireland) completed its breastworks "about noon" on 2 Jul (the regiment had marched "early on the morning of Thursday, July 2" to the right of the road to Gettysburg).
subclaims.why: Regimental report in the Official Records. The web lead of the printed row (Gettysburg Daily, "about noon") is not needed and is not used.

subclaims.claim: The 60th NY (Col. Godard) worked at its intrenchments from about 06:00 "until about 9 a. m., by that time completing the intrenchments", by Greene's order.
subclaims.why: Regimental report in the Official Records; with the 137th NY (noon) it gives two documented finish values inside Greene's brigade, both carried as selectable scenarios.

subclaims.claim: The stone wall behind the First Division's line existed before the division arrived on 2 Jul and is most probably a farm field wall: the First Brigade formed "behind a stone wall" and only then "immediately built breastworks" in front of it (McDougall), and the 145th NY was "repairing the stone wall" (Price); no local source describes the wall's origin, owner or builder.
subclaims.why: The two OR passages show a wall standing before any Union work; that it was a farm field wall of 1863 (not built by Union troops earlier that morning) is an inference. The NPS texts read here describe the stone-walled fields of East Cemetery Hill but do not locate a wall behind the Culp's Hill line.

sub_requirement_text: State-schedule entry S-024 changes state at its documented window.
corrected_claim: Culp's Hill, 2 Jul: the printed "morning" fits Geary's division (05:00, regiments 04:00-06:00) but not the rest. Kane's brigade arrived at 06:00 and built its breastwork "before sundown" (no morning hour); the First Division received its orders at 08:00 and about 09:00 and McDougall's brigade built "immediately" after being withdrawn at about 11:00, finishing in the afternoon (first-line regiments still building at 18:30); Wadsworth's division began a temporary breastwork on the hill on the afternoon and evening of 1 Jul. On 3 Jul the 147th PA charged the stone wall held by the enemy at 05:00 after the 03:45 bombardment (Geary, Candy).

subclaims.claim: The First Division's works: Williams's corps order came "At 8 a. m."; Ruger "About 9 a. m." was ordered to move the division to the right of the Second Division; the First Brigade, held at an earlier position "until about 11 a. m.", was withdrawn, formed in the woods and "immediately built breastworks" (McDougall); the 123rd NY built a strong breastwork in the front line, the 46th PA finished its breastworks "in the afternoon", and the first-line regiments were still "building breastworks" at 18:30 (Price); the 5th CT says it began breastworks in the morning after 04:00. The printed "Jul 2 morning" is therefore not supported as a start hour for the First Brigade: the documented starts are the orders at about 09:00 and the withdrawal at about 11:00, and the 5th CT's own "morning" after 04:00 is at an unnamed position.
subclaims.why: Regiment and brigade hours differ (5th CT morning after 04:00; McDougall about 11:00 then immediately; 46th PA afternoon); the sector window is carried as a range, not a point.

subclaims.claim: Geary's division was placed in line "At 5 a. m. on the 2d" and "Breastworks were immediately thrown up along our entire line" (Geary); his three brigades' regiments give 04:00 to 06:00 for their start (see S-023 for Greene's).
Kane's brigade, ordered into line "soon after" he assumed command at 06:00 on 2 Jul, threw up its breastwork "before sundown"; Kane gives no morning hour.
subclaims.why: Kane's own report; it bounds the Kane-sector work between 06:00 and sundown and does not support the printed "Jul 2 morning" for that sector (the same conflict is carried at fence-1 E-07).

subclaims.claim: Wadsworth's division (I Corps) began works on the hill on the afternoon and evening of 1 Jul, not on the morning of 2 Jul: the 7th Indiana "took up a position on the hill east of Gettysburg, forming at that time the extreme right of our lines" and "immediately commenced the construction of a temporary breastwork" (Grover), the 6th Wisconsin was directed by Wadsworth to "Culp's Hill" (Dawes), and the 95th NY "occupied the intrenchments on the right" on 2 Jul (Pye).
subclaims.why: The identity of Grover's "hill east of Gettysburg" and Pye's "intrenchments on the right" with Culp's Hill rests on Dawes naming that hill for the same division; no report states hours of building on 2 Jul.

subclaims.claim: At 05:00 on 3 Jul the 147th PA (Candy's brigade), which after several rounds from a battery that opened at 03:45 had been "ordered forward" and "occupied a stone fence in front of the enemy" (Candy), was "ordered to charge and carry the stone wall occupied by the enemy", which the enemy "then abandoned" along its whole line (Geary); Geary places this wall at the lane in front of Candy's brigade, "the stone wall previously mentioned" (the wall 200 yd behind Kane's works held by the enemy since the night of 2 Jul).
subclaims.why: Candy's "stone fence" and Geary's "stone wall" are not equated in words; they are the same movement of the same regiment and Geary's own text ties the wall to the lane in front of Candy's brigade, so the identity is carried as documented only for Geary's wall.

subclaims.claim: Wall behind the line: see S-023 (six witnesses, two groups).

printed.object: Culp's Hill traverse and extra head logs

corrected_claim: Culp's Hill traverse: Greene's own 1893 address documents a traverse of about twenty yards commenced by the 137th NY on the right of the brigade (after the breastwork was finished, no hour) and used at about 22:00; "early in the day" belongs to the breastwork, not to the traverse. Extra head logs have no source in the local texts (only 1864 campaigns mention head logs).

subclaims.claim: The 137th NY (Col. Ireland) commenced a traverse on the right of the Third Brigade's line, extended about twenty yards and "of great value during the subsequent fight"; Greene mentions it after saying that the breastwork "was completed early in the day", without an hour for the traverse; at about 22:00 the 137th, forced back from Kane's works "to the traverse on our right", "reformed in good order and maintained their position" there (Greene 1893). Ireland's own 1863 report speaks of forming "on the prolongation of the works".
subclaims.why: Greene's 1893 address (retrospective by the brigade commander); the 1863 reports do not use the word "traverse". The statement that the traverse was begun "early in the day" of the printed row is not in the source: only the breastwork is said to be completed early.

subclaims.claim: Extra head logs were added through 2 Jul.
subclaims.why: No local text says it. The PDF source is the DMNA 60th NY page and HistoryNet "King of the Hill" (web pages, not reachable).

subclaims.claim: The traverse was begun on 2 Jul and stood by the night attack: Greene mentions it after saying that the breastwork "was completed early in the day" and before the "subsequent fight"; the 137th NY completed its own breastworks "about noon" and was attacked from "About 7 p. m." (Ireland), so the work falls between about noon and 19:00 by inference; no source dates the traverse itself.
subclaims.why: Sequence in Greene's address plus the hours of the 137th NY's own report; the printed window "morning through the day" is not supported.

printed.time: Between Jul 1 evening and 16:00 Jul 2 (I; builder unknown)

corrected_claim: East Cemetery Hill: light per-gun earthworks were thrown up at dusk on 1 Jul (Wainwright, Hunt) and Wiedrich's battery built redans or lunettes for each gun with its own men; they stood at the 21:00 assault of 2 Jul. The printed 16:00 limit of 2 Jul is not documented either way. Stone walls on each side of a lane below the battery and stone-and-plank/board fences on the ascent are documented for the evening of 2 Jul.

subclaims.claim: Light/small earthworks stood in front of each gun of the batteries outside the cemetery gate by dusk on 1 Jul.
subclaims.why: Wainwright, commanding the Artillery Brigade, First Corps; Hunt, Chief of Artillery. Builders: the passages do not name the builders (the batteries' own men are implied by "to protect the men").

subclaims.claim: The works were lunettes (or redans), built "for each gun" by the battery's own men on East Cemetery Hill after the retreat of 1 Jul (Wiedrich's battery, NY vol. 3); the NPS also names a July 1863 photograph "Lunette earthworks across from Evergreen Cemetery".
subclaims.why: A participant battery history (retrospective, 1902) gives form, builder and place; the OR (Wainwright, Hunt) says only "light"/"small" earthworks, so the form rests on one regimental source and the NPS caption.

subclaims.claim: Built after the battery took position on 1 Jul (works "at dusk", Wainwright; "now commenced", NY vol. 3) and standing at about 21:00 on 2 Jul, when a Confederate "planted his colors on one of the lunettes of the first section"; builder: the battery's own men. The printed upper limit of 16:00 on 2 Jul is neither supported nor contradicted.
subclaims.why: The documented window runs from the evening of 1 Jul to at least 21:00 on 2 Jul; no source dates a completion hour.

subclaims.claim: Stone walls on each side of a lane below the battery (17th CT, about 19:00 on 2 Jul); stone and plank/board fences on the ascent under the Confederate attack (Early, Lee); the Confederates were seen climbing walls and fences at the base of Benner's Hill at 19:45 (5th Maine Battery).
Cannoneers of Wiedrich's and Ricketts' batteries drove the attackers off with fence-rails and stones.
subclaims.why: That the rails came from fences on the hill is implied, not stated.

corrected_claim: Weikert farm (Jacob Weikert, Taneytown road): wounded were already in the barn on the evening of 1 Jul (Tillie Pierce, 1889) and the V Corps hospital is named at the house and barns of J. Weikart during the afternoon cannonade of 3 Jul, moved afterwards to Bushman's (NY vol. 3); the NPS (1988) calls the buildings field hospitals during and after the battle. The printed "morning of 2 Jul, surgeons arrive" has no source.

subclaims.claim: The Weikert farm buildings (Jacob Weikert, on the Taneytown road at the eastern slope of Round Top) were used as field hospitals: wounded were brought to the house and the barn filled before night on 1 Jul, with nurses in the basement kitchen (Tillie Pierce, 1889); the NPS (1988) says the buildings "were used as field hospitals during and after the battle for the casualties at Little Round Top and the Wheatfield Road".
subclaims.why: NPS secondary statement (undated within the battle) plus an eyewitness of the first night (a child witness, published 1889, retrospective): the first use is the evening of 1 Jul, earlier than the printed "morning of 2 Jul".

subclaims.claim: A V Corps hospital was "made at the house and barns of J. Weikart, on the Taneytown Road, at the foot of the east front of Little Round Top" and was still there during the afternoon cannonade of 3 Jul, when shells struck it; it was then moved to Lewis Bushman's, about a mile to the southeast (regimental narrative, NY vol. 3). The hour of its opening on 2 Jul ("morning", "surgeons arrive") is not stated.
subclaims.why: A single 1902 regimental narrative names the corps and the house; no hour of opening, no surgeon and no date before 3 Jul is given.

printed.to_state: Artillery duel; Confederate guns driven off

corrected_claim: Benner's Hill, 2 Jul about 15:30-16:00: Andrews' battalion (Maj. Latimer) came into action with fourteen guns on the hill and two 20-pounder Parrotts in rear (Confederate report, "About 4 o'clock" by the page image; Maine narrative); the Union reports date the Confederate battery of four 20-pounders and six 10-pounder Parrotts to 15:30 (Hunt) and 16:00 (Wainwright). The length of the duel is carried as four values (under 30 min, an hour or more, 1.5 h, until near night). At 19:45 Confederate infantry climbed walls and fences at the base of the hill (Maine).

subclaims.claim: Andrews' battalion (Maj. Latimer) came into action on Benner's Hill with fourteen guns on the hill and two 20-pounder Parrotts on an eminence in rear (Confederate report); the Union side dates it to about 15:30-16:00: the 5th Maine narrative "About 4 p. M." (the battery came into view), Hunt "At about 3.30 p. m." (a battery of ten guns, four 20-pounders and six 10-pounder Parrotts, in a wheat-field east of Cemetery Hill) and Wainwright "about 4 p. m." (the same battery); the Confederate order is "About 4 o'clock" (Andrews; the text file's OCR prints "-1", the page image reads 4; no a.m. or p.m. is printed, afternoon by the sequence and the Union hours). The identification of Hunt's and Wainwright's battery with Latimer's battalion is inferred from place and hour (Benner's Hill is not named).
subclaims.why: Hour range 15:30 (Hunt) to 16:00 (Maine, Wainwright, Andrews); the Confederate digit is read from the page image. Greene 1893 (c3) is about the Union artillery on Culp's Hill driving the Benner's Hill batteries under cover at about 4 o'clock.

corrected_claim: Rose/Slyder/Bushman ground, 2 Jul: Kershaw formed his brigade at about 15:00 in front of a stone wall, then behind it (division along the wall); at about 16:00 numerous fences lay in the way and a stone house and barn stood about 500 yd ahead, which the NPS treats as the Rose farm buildings; the Rose yard picket fence was an obstacle (NPS, Tipton photographs). subclaims.claim: A stone wall stood at the Confederate start line; Kershaw's brigade formed in front of and then behind it at about 15:00 on 2 Jul, and the division formed along it with artillery to the right.

A stone house and, to its left, a stone barn stood about 500 yd in front of Kershaw's centre, with a stone wall running parallel to his line on the right and a morass behind the house (Kershaw); the NPS Record of Treatment places Kershaw's advance "to the farm buildings of George and Catharine Rose" and quotes his view "from the stone house".
subclaims.why: Kershaw does not name the Rose farm; the NPS frames his stone house as one of the Rose farm buildings (implicit, institutional secondary). The OR gives the layout and distances.

subclaims.claim: About 16:00 ("about 4 o'clock, when I received orders to advance") "The numerous fences in the way, the stone building and barn, and the morass" made it difficult for Kershaw's brigade to keep its line (Kershaw); the NPS adds that the picket fencing of the Rose yard and garden "created an obstacle to Confederate forces" (photographs of the Tipton Collection); no fence removal is documented for Kershaw's brigade, the line crossed under fire.
The Rose house, Rose barn, Bushman barn and Slyder house served as Confederate cover and hospital (Bushman: 8 buried).
subclaims.why: No local primary or NPS statement found; PDF keys SS-Rose, SS-Bushman, SS-Slyder are Stone Sentinels leads.

subclaims.claim: On the afternoon of 2 Jul a rail fence stood in the way of the 3rd Arkansas (Robertson's brigade) advancing east from the Snyder farmstead and Longstreet ordered the front line: "Grab the bottom rail and turn it over, when you get to it" (a soldier's recollection quoted by the NPS); the NPS places such worm fences along the Emmitsburg Road or the west boundaries of Snyder Fields 3 and 7.
subclaims.why: Quoted second-hand from a soldier's recollection (footnote 30 of the NPS report, not read); the place of the fence is the NPS's inference ("may have referred to"); documents a rail-turning removal technique for one regiment, not for the Rose Farm fences.

subclaims.claim: Soldiers of Semmes's Brigade were buried in the Rose farm orchard near the springhouse ("Jno Roses Place orchard, near fence"), according to a local physician's list of Confederate interments of 1864 (as reported by the NPS).
subclaims.why: Second-hand: the NPS report summarises the interments list; it concerns burials after the battle, not the Rose buildings' use as hospital or cover.

subclaims.claim: The Wheatfield ground was fenced and walled on 2 Jul: stone fences and walls (Sweitzer: "the stone fence beyond the wheat-field next to the woods"; Crawford; de Trobriand; Burbank; Brooke; Kershaw: the enemy line "posted behind a stone wall" in rear of the field) and a fence round the field itself: the 61st NY (Cross's brigade), in the afternoon, "In front of us across the road was a wheatfeld, which was bounded by fence ... we scaled the fence and advanced" (NPS quoting a participant), and the NPS documents the north and west perimeter as a wooden fence in the 1863 Bachelder Map; which wall is which is not established.
subclaims.why: Which wall is which is not established by any text; the layout stays open (fence-2-EG-06).

subclaims.claim: The field carried standing grain before the fight: "peach and apple orchards adjoined fields of ripening wheat" in the community before the battle (a Massachusetts captain, quoted in the NPS inventory); Haskell: "the ripening grain" in the fields in view on 2 Jul; Hall: "full-grown wheat" in the district on 1 Jul; the field is called a "wheat-field" by Kershaw, Sweitzer and de Trobriand.
subclaims.why: None of the passages names the Wheatfield as carrying ripe wheat; the NPS inventory passage is about the Emmitsburg Road ridge community.

subclaims.claim: Crops were trampled and wheat destroyed in the battle: Haskell "the harvest trodden in the mud" (evening of 2 Jul, fields behind the fight); the NPS summary of the battlefield after the battle ("crops were trampled"); damage claims of John Slyder (5-7 acres of wheat) and Michael Bushman (wheat among other crops) on the adjoining fields (NPS); no source gives the Wheatfield's own wheat loss or the 16:30 start.
subclaims.why: General or neighbouring statements only; the Rose damage claim and the Wheatfield itself are not named in a local text.

subclaims.claim: The wheat was clipped by fire.
subclaims.why: Only a front-matter poem in Pennsylvania at Gettysburg (not a source) says the wheat was "clipped"; PDF notes "a forum citing Pfanz".

corrected_claim: Peach Orchard/Sherfy fences, 2 Jul: a rail fence stood 30-40 rods west of the Emmitsburg road on the night of 1-2 Jul; Union troops pulled down fences and walls from after midnight to about 11:00 (26th PA, 86th NY, in front of Humphreys's division; cleared by about 09:00 at the orchard); the orchard's own south and east fence stood in the afternoon (3rd Maine to about 16:00, 110th PA before 15:30, 2nd NH, Thompson's battery at Sherfy's stable and garden fence after 16:30, road fence at the Sherfy house); rails lay in the orchard at about 01:00 on 3 Jul. The printed "destroyed afternoon-evening 2 Jul" has no source.

subclaims.claim: A rail fence ran 30-40 rods west of the Emmitsburg road and was the 4th Maine's picket line on the night of 1-2 Jul; Union pickets held the Sherfy western fence and hedgerow.

Union troops pulled down fences on 2 Jul before the Peach Orchard fight: the 26th PA tore down "the fences between the Baltimore pike and the Emmitsburg road" after its midnight arrival (regimental narrative) and Bodine reports it "detailed to clear away the fences in front of the division" in the morning; the 86th NY, after 10:00, sent 35 men under Capt. Baker "to demolish all stone walls and fences in our front to the Emmitsburg road", back at about 11:00; a New York battery arriving at 09:00 "noticed that the fences had been cleared away" near the Peach Orchard; Humphreys: fences "removing such of the fences as were in the way" (no hour); an anonymous letter in Meade's report says Sickles had "leveling all the fences and stone walls" done (partisan).
subclaims.why: Two independent OR reports (Bodine, Higgins) plus the 26th PA regimental narrative (same regiment as Bodine) and a battery witness. The Humphreys passage has no hour; R006 is partisan. NPS (2024): "Although Union forces removed many of the north-south fences prior to the second day's battle".

subclaims.claim: Some fences still stood around the Peach Orchard and Sherfy buildings in the afternoon of 2 Jul: the 3rd Maine waited "behind the fence that bounded the Peach Orchard" on the southwest side until about 16:00; the 110th PA took position "inside of the peach orchard fence" for a few minutes before 15:30; the 2nd NH, "During the afternoon of July 2", stood behind the fence on the south side of the orchard (NPS quoting its narrative; the worm fence on the south and east sides is on the 1863 Bachelder Map); Thompson's battery from about 16:30 placed one gun between "Sherfy's stable and garden fence" and the Emmitsburg road; the 114th PA, after about two hours under artillery fire, "clambered over the fence" on the Emmitsburg road at the Sherfy house (no clock hour).
subclaims.why: Each hour is inside the quote or its widened span, except the 114th PA (after about two hours of shelling, no hour) and the NPS 2nd NH statement (afternoon).

printed.to_state: Hart fires from about 16:30; canister about 17:30

corrected_claim: Hart's battery (15th NY) took position on the left (south line) of the Peach Orchard on Hunt's order and fired canister against the 8th South Carolina column; the brigade was ordered to Sickles at about 15:30 and Phillips went into action at 16:00; Hart's fire against infantry falls between about 17:00 and 17:45 by inference (McGilvery); the printed 16:30 and 17:30 are not in any source. The battery at Sherfy's stable and garden fence was Thompson's, not Hart's.

subclaims.claim: Hart's 15th NY Battery took position on the left of the peach orchard on Hunt's order (Hart), "on the south line of the Peach Orchard" (NY vol. 1); it fired on an enemy battery at about 900 yards, then on a heavy column of infantry with shrapnel and canister, "repulsing the attack made on my battery" (Hart); the 141st PA, supporting it, names the attacker as the 8th South Carolina.

Hart's report gives no clock hour. The brigade got its order at about 15:30 (McGilvery), the neighbouring battery of Phillips was ordered into action "At 4 o'clock", a heavy column of infantry appeared in front of the line of batteries "At about 5 o'clock" and the infantry took the woods on the left "At about a quarter to 6" (McGilvery); Hart's canister fire against infantry therefore falls between about 17:00 and 17:45 by inference; the printed 16:30 (start) and 17:30 (canister) are neither supported nor contradicted.
subclaims.why: Brigade-level hours from McGilvery and Phillips bracket Hart's fire; his own report names no time.

subclaims.claim: McGilvery received the order for Sickles about 15:30; Phillips' battery went into action about 16:00.

Another battery of the brigade (Thompson), ordered to the Peach Orchard "about 4.30 o'clock p. m.", put one gun between "Sherfy's stable and garden fence" and the Emmitsburg road; its guns were in position about twenty minutes before the left and centre sections opened; the Peach Orchard fence stood with infantry behind it until about 16:00 (3rd Maine). Hart's own gun line is not tied to any fence in the sources read.
subclaims.why: Hart's own gun line is not tied to any fence in the sources read.

corrected_claim: The Sherfy barn burned after the 2 Jul evening fight with badly wounded and dead men of the 114th PA inside (114th PA narrative, Bowen, Bachelder, 1867 cemetery report); a Confederate officer was in it just before it burned (Bachelder); Hart (OR) claims on 3 Jul to have set "the barn" on fire by his fire on a Confederate battery. The date (2 Jul evening or 3 Jul) and cause stay a registered conflict (C-026).

subclaims.claim: The Sherfy barn burned with badly wounded men of the 114th PA inside, who had taken refuge there during the 2 Jul evening fight (114th PA narrative); Bowen (OR) reports men missing "whom I have no doubt were killed and their bodies burned when the barn was burned down"; Bachelder (1873): "His barn was burned, and many bodies of dead Union soldiers were consumed with it"; the 1867 cemetery report lists unknown Zouaves "(burned" ... "Sherfy's barn".
subclaims.why: The burning therefore came after those men were wounded on the evening of 2 Jul; none of these passages dates it. Bowen does not name the barn; the cemetery table is OCR-interleaved.

subclaims.claim: No source dates the fire. Evidence bearing on it: the wounded were in the barn after the evening fight of 2 Jul (114th PA); a Confederate officer says he was "personally in the barn immediately before it was burned" (Bachelder; he does not say whether the barn was then in Confederate hands); Hart (OR) claims that on 3 Jul his fire exploded the caissons of a Confederate battery "in front of a barn" and "set the barn on fire" (the barn is not named). Both windows (2 Jul evening, 3 Jul during the afternoon artillery) stay selectable (conflict C-026) and so do the causes (Union shell fire, per Hart; ignition by shells; Confederate).
subclaims.why: The sources fix a lower bound (after the 2 Jul evening fight) and one claimed cause and time (Hart, 3 Jul); they do not decide the conflict.

printed.to_state: Hazlett's guns hauled up; first fire 17:45

corrected_claim: Little Round Top, 2 Jul: Hazlett's battery went up behind the 140th NY after about 16:00 and into battery on the summit; Hunt dates the move to Round Top at about 16:30 and says it opened immediately, which replaces the printed first fire at 17:45; Hazlett fell about an hour into the action and died at 20:00. The retrospective accounts disagree on how the guns were got up (by hand or by teams). The works on the hill were stone breastworks of boulders built that night and the next morning; no rail use is documented, and the present walls were restacked in 1882-1887.

subclaims.claim: Hazlett's Battery D, 5th US, ascended Little Round Top behind the 140th NY and went into battery on the summit after the brigade moved forward about 16:00 (Garrard); Hunt: "About 4.30 p. m. Hazlett's battery was moved to the extreme left, placed in position on Round Top, and immediately opened"; Martin: the Fifth Corps artillery "entered the field between 4 and 5 p. m.".
The guns were got up the slope by hand with the infantry (155th PA; 20th Maine address) or by teams with the drivers (140th NY volume).
subclaims.why: The retrospective accounts differ; both carried as scenarios (no default).

subclaims.claim: The battery fired its first round at 17:45 (printed).
subclaims.why: Not supported: Hunt (OR) places the battery in position at about 16:30 and says it "immediately opened"; no source gives 17:45. The sub-claim below carries the documented hours.

subclaims.claim: Rails or fences were used on Little Round Top itself (printed): no local source; the NPS says the boulder-strewn slopes "provided Union infantry ample materials to build stone breastworks during the night of July 2 and morning of July 3", and a photograph of 6 Jul 1863 shows the stone breastworks on the summit; the present walls were restacked by the GBMA in 1882-1887 and "sometimes did not resemble their wartime appearance".
subclaims.why: The open part is rail use; the cited NPS statements document stone breastworks of boulders, not rails.

subclaims.claim: Hunt places the move to Round Top at about 16:30 with the battery opening "immediately" and firing "until night"; Rittenhouse says the battery "had been engaged only about an hour" when Hazlett was shot, and that he died at 20:00; the exact hour of the first round is not stated.
subclaims.why: Two OR statements bracket the first fire (about 16:30) and the wounding of Hazlett (about an hour after the first fire); no source gives the minute.

corrected_claim: Bigelow's 9th Massachusetts Battery retired by prolonge 300 yd (Milton) after the infantry gave way about 17:45 (McGilvery) to a position near two stone walls meeting at an obtuse angle, held there at all hazards, and lost four guns when enveloped; the NPS ties the walls to the Trostle farm wall and gate and the capture to the 21st Mississippi. subclaims.claim: Bigelow's battery retired by prolonge, firing canister, 300 yd (Milton) after the infantry gave way at about 17:45 (McGilvery); McGilvery ordered the batteries generally to "retire 350 yards" and formed a new artillery line "about 400 yards to the rear".

subclaims.claim: The battery stood at a position near which two stone walls met at an obtuse angle, ordered to hold at all hazards without infantry support under enfilading fire.

The flanks closed in; the four pieces on the right were silenced and left (Milton, McGilvery: "forced to leave four guns and retire"); the survivors withdrew a mile and a half and went into park at 21:00 (Milton) and the four guns were recovered the same day.
The walls are the Trostle farm stone wall with its narrow gate, which stayed standing and, with an overturned limber, trapped four guns taken by the 21st Mississippi.
subclaims.why: Institutional secondary (NPS inventory); the OR reports do not name the Trostle farm for the walls.

subclaims.claim: The guns were overrun at about 18:30.
subclaims.why: After "a quarter to 6" (McGilvery) and before the 21:00 park (Milton); no report gives 18:30.

corrected_claim: At about 18:30 on 2 Jul the Twelfth Corps units left Greene's right and Greene, alone, was ordered to hold the whole line of intrenchments, spacing his men thin: "about a foot between each man" (Greene 1893), "single file, with intervening spaces of a foot or more" (Stegman, 102nd NY, shortly after 18:00) and "one man deep" (Ireland, 137th NY); the 300 and 800 yd lengths are unsupported (blog source).

Greene's brigade spread its line thin: "leaving about a foot between each man in the breastworks" (Greene 1893); in the 1863 reports the 102nd NY "Shortly after 6 p. m." was moved to the 149th NY's intrenchments "the men forming in single file, with intervening spaces of a foot or more" (Stegman), and the 137th NY, ordered into the works of Kane's brigade, "had to form line one man deep" (Ireland); the morning works of the 60th, 102nd and 149th NY formed "a long and continuous breastwork" (Stegman).
The line was about 300 yd in the morning, then about 800 yd after 18:30.
subclaims.why: Only the Gettysburg Daily blog (GD-219); no OR or regimental text gives yards for the line.

subclaims.claim: Weed's brigade (Garrard) strengthened the Round Top ridge at night with a stone wall about half way down the slope wherever the rocks gave no protection.
subclaims.why: Hour: "at night" (the PDF's about 20:00 is inferred and has no source).

subclaims.claim: Fisher took the 5th and 12th Pennsylvania Reserves and the 20th Maine up the hill (Big Round Top) at 22:00 on 2 Jul and, "In the morning" of 3 Jul, changed his position to cover the ravine between the two hills and "at once threw up a stone wall across the entire ravine and up the hill".
subclaims.why: A different wall (the ravine between the two Round Tops) built by different units on 3 Jul morning; carried with the Weed/Garrard wall as two builders, not one.

subclaims.claim: A stone fence inclosing a wood stood in front of the hill; the 7th US Infantry (formed "at about 5.30 p. m.") "remained some minutes under cover of a stone fence inclosing a wood" (Capt. Hancock).

subclaims.why: Not stated by any source read.

subclaims.claim: The Union infantry built the stone breastworks of the boulders of the slopes (NPS: the slopes "provided Union infantry ample materials to build stone breastworks during the night of July 2 and morning of July 3"); the NPS statement of the 1930s says stone walls on the south side of Little Round Top "were erected and used by the Union forces".
subclaims.why: NPS statements (secondary): the boulders are the material, no source says the walls reused stone from an existing field wall.

subclaims.claim: The present stone walls on the summit were restacked by the GBMA in 1882-1887 and "sometimes did not resemble their wartime appearance"; they are not a source for the 1863 profiles.

corrected_claim: Evergreen Cemetery: fences in the grounds were smashed by the cannonade of about 13:00 on 3 Jul (Howard); contemporary newspapers (20-21 Jul 1863) report railings and ornamental work around the lots "somewhat shattered" and tombstones thrown down or broken; a July 1863 visitor found the iron railings "bent and broken into the smallest pieces" and the highest monuments deliberately laid down by the soldiers; no primary dates the iron-fence destruction to 2 Jul, though the hill was bombarded that afternoon.

subclaims.claim: On 3 Jul ("July 3, at 5 a. m. ...") "At about 1 p. m. a terrific cannonade opened upon us from the west, northwest, north, and northeast, hurling into the cemetery grounds missiles of every description" and the shells burst "overturning tombstones, and smashing fences"; the cannonade ceased at 15:30 (Howard).
subclaims.why: Howard, XI Corps and the commander on the hill; date 3 Jul by the report's own sequence (the cannonade ended at 15:30).

subclaims.claim: The newspapers report: tombstones erected over graves thrown from their position or broken, graves turned up by ploughing shot, and tasteful railings and other ornamental work around the lots somewhat shattered (Evergreen Cemetery, Cemetery Hill).
subclaims.why: Gettysburg Compiler 20 Jul 1863 and Adams Sentinel 21 Jul 1863 print the same sentences; the text is read from the three-column OCR in which the lines of one column are separated by lines of the others, so each quoted fragment is a contiguous OCR line run and the join is editorial; undated within the battle.

subclaims.claim: Iron railings were "bent and broken into the smallest pieces" and the soldiers had carefully laid down the highest monuments (not toppled by fire).
subclaims.why: Visitor's account (1864); contradicts "obelisks toppled" of the printed row for the laying-down of the tall monuments; NPS CLR says General Howard ordered the headstones laid flat to prevent destruction.

subclaims.claim: On the evening of 2 Jul, after the fight on the Union left, fences lay prostrate and the harvest was trodden in the mud over the fields Haskell saw ("They were beautiful this morning. They are desolate now").
subclaims.why: Participant letter written in July 1863; not the cemetery by name; the fields are those of the Third Corps fight.

subclaims.claim: Plank fences along Baltimore Pike and grave-plot fences were damaged or removed; most fences of the adjoining fields were probably taken down.
subclaims.why: Institutional secondary; "probably" in the second quotation.

subclaims.claim: Cemetery Hill was under heavy bombardment on the afternoon of 2 Jul from about 16:00 for two hours ("At about 4 p. m. the enemy's batteries opened a heavy fire upon our position, which lasted for two hours", Steinwehr), with the stone fences protecting the infantry; Dobke: "All remained quiet until 4 p. m. of July 2, when the enemy's batteries opened ... concentrating their fire on Cemetery Hill"; a possible source of 2 Jul damage.

subclaims.claim: General Weed was in the basement room of the Weikert house on the evening of 2 Jul, alive and speaking (Tillie Pierce), and "dead" there when she came down after the sun was high on 3 Jul: "This is the body of General Weed"; the volume's plate caption says "Mortally wounded on Little Round Top, July 2nd, 1863. The hour of death is not stated ("before dawn" is not in the text); the printed "hospital moves east early on 3 Jul" is contradicted for the V Corps hospital by NY vol. 3, which moves it to Bushman's after the afternoon cannonade of 3 Jul.
subclaims.why: One eyewitness (a child, published 1889) and the volume's own caption; place and night documented, hour unknown; the move is dated by a regimental narrative.

corrected_claim: Culp's Hill, 3 Jul: the Union artillery opened at 03:30 (Geary, "early dawn"), 04:00 (Greene), 04:30 (Hunt, Muhlenberg) or daylight (Williams) with a ten- to fifteen-minute burst, again at 05:30 with five batteries (20 guns at 04:30, 26 from 05:30; Geary's 14 separate) firing at intervals until about 10:00; the 147th PA occupied a stone fence after the 03:45 battery fire and was ordered at 05:00 to carry the wall; the 3rd Wisconsin lay behind a rail breastwork at daybreak. Damage to the works is not documented.

subclaims.claim: The first Union artillery burst on the enemy in the intrenchments is dated 03:30 "(early dawn)" with a ten-minute artillery fire (Geary), "At 4 a. m." (Greene), "At 4.30 a. m." for fifteen minutes (Hunt, Muhlenberg) and "at daylight" for fifteen minutes (Williams): four start values carried as scenarios; Geary adds a second burst after twenty minutes of about fifteen minutes, and Hunt and Muhlenberg a second phase from 05:30 ("at 5.30 a. m. all the batteries opened") firing at intervals until 10:00.
subclaims.why: The OR gives four different start hours (03:30, 04:00, 04:30, daylight); none is chosen. The printed "30 min to 3 hours" window is not an OR value: the documented durations are 10-15 minutes for the first burst and 05:30-10:00 at intervals for the second phase.

subclaims.claim: Hunt names five batteries on the hill with their guns: Knap (E, Pennsylvania, six 10-pounders), Winegar (M, 1st New York, four 10-pounders), Muhlenberg (F, 4th US, six 12-pounders), Kinzie (K, 5th US, four 12-pounders) and Rigby (A, Maryland, six 3-inch): the first four, 20 guns, were in place by 04:30 (Muhlenberg counts "ten guns" of two rifled and "ten guns" of two light 12-pounder batteries at 04:30) and Rigby's battery was added "soon after daylight" so that "all the batteries" (26 by Hunt's types) opened at 05:30; Geary says Muhlenberg "reported with fourteen pieces" (an earlier count not reconciled with the others); the printed "24 guns" matches none.
subclaims.why: 20 guns at 04:30 and 26 from 05:30 are consistent (Rigby's six added); Geary's fourteen and the printed 24 stay as separate values.

subclaims.claim: The 147th PA occupied a stone fence in front of the enemy after the 03:45 shelling and was ordered at 05:00 to carry the stone wall held by the enemy.
At daybreak the 3rd Wisconsin lay behind a hastily erected breastwork of rails on the Culp's Hill right.
The works were damaged by the shelling (splintered head logs, shell craters behind).
subclaims.why: No OR text describes damage to the works: Hunt, Muhlenberg, Geary, Greene and Williams record where the fire fell (the wood and ravine at 600-800 yd, the enemy in the intrenchments), not damage to the breastworks; the printed claim is marked inferred in the plan and has no source.

corrected_claim: Bliss house and barn, 3 Jul: still held by Confederate skirmishers at 07:30; Hays ordered them burned in the lull between about 11:00 and about 14:00, Smyth passed the order and the 14th Connecticut fired them in several places; the barn was ruins by late afternoon. The "morning, before the cannonade" window is narrowed to about 11:00-14:00.

subclaims.claim: Hays ordered the house and barn in his front burned; Smyth's brigade passed the order and the 14th Connecticut set them on fire in several places after removing its killed and wounded.
The burning came after the lull began at about 11:00 and before about 14:00 on 3 Jul (the cannonade); the barn still sheltered Confederate skirmishers and was cleared at 07:30 that morning.
subclaims.why: The printed "Morning Jul 3 (late morning per one forum)" is bounded by Hays: after about 11:00 and before nearly 14:00; the 07:30 report shows the barn standing and occupied in the early morning.

subclaims.claim: The barn was a ruin by late afternoon of 3 Jul: Dent's regiment was "ordered to charge on the ruins of the burnt barn in our front" "Late in the afternoon of the third day"; Posey: his regiments advanced in the afternoon "beyond the barn and house, which were burned".

The "house and barn in our front" are the Bliss house and barn: the OR reports do not name Bliss; the New Jersey commission names "the Bliss barn site" as the land bought by the Society of the 14th Connecticut "in memory of an incident of the battle in which they were the chief actors" and the Bliss barn and house as taken by the 12th NJ on the second and third of July (retrospective, 1891); the NPS: "Bliss Farm, burned on the third day of the battle".
subclaims.why: Identification by two retrospective sources (state commission report, NPS plan); neither OR passage names the farm.

subclaims.claim: The fires were set with hay, straw and cartridge paper.
subclaims.why: No local text gives materials.
